title: Breakdown of Pyruvate

source_sentences.text: In order for pyruvate, the product of glycolysis, to enter the next pathway, it must undergo several changes.
The conversion is a three-step process (Figure 7.10).
Step 1. A carboxyl group is removed from pyruvate, releasing a molecule of carbon dioxide into the surrounding medium.
This reaction creates a two-carbon hydroxyethyl group bound to the enzyme (pyruvate dehydrogenase).
We should note that this is the first of the six carbons from the original glucose molecule to be removed.

(This step proceeds twice because there are two pyruvate molecules produced at the end of glycolysis for every molecule of glucose metabolized anaerobically; thus, two of the six carbons will have been removed at the end of both steps.)
Step 2. The hydroxyethyl group is oxidized to an acetyl group, and the electrons are picked up by NAD+, forming NADH.
Step 3. The enzyme-bound acetyl group is transferred to CoA, producing a molecule of acetyl CoA.

expert.text: To enter the next pathway, pyruvate, which is the product of glycolysis, must undergo a three-step conversion process.
In Step 1, a carboxyl group is removed from pyruvate, releasing carbon dioxide and creating a two-carbon hydroxyethyl group bound to pyruvate dehydrogenase.
This represents the first of the six carbons from the original glucose molecule to be removed, occurring twice per glucose molecule as two pyruvates are formed.
In Step 2, the hydroxyethyl group is oxidized into an acetyl group, transferring electrons to NAD+ to form NADH.
In Step 3, the enzyme-bound acetyl group is transferred to CoA, generating acetyl CoA.

grade10.text: Pyruvate from glycolysis must undergo three key steps before moving to the next pathway.
First, a carboxyl group is removed from pyruvate, releasing carbon dioxide gas.
This leaves a two-carbon hydroxyethyl group attached to the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase.
Because one glucose splits into two pyruvates, this step occurs twice and removes two carbon atoms.
Second, the hydroxyethyl group is oxidized to an acetyl group, converting NAD+ to NADH.
Finally, the acetyl group attaches to CoA, forming acetyl CoA.

grade6.text: Pyruvate needs three steps to get ready for the next process.
First, it loses carbon dioxide gas into its surroundings.
This leaves a small two-carbon piece attached to an enzyme.
Since glucose makes two pyruvates, this step happens twice.
Next, energy electrons are added to NAD+ to make NADH.
Finally, the piece connects to CoA to form acetyl CoA.

glossary.plain: A three-carbon molecule produced at the end of glycolysis.
The initial metabolic pathway that breaks down glucose to release energy.
An enzyme complex that helps break down pyruvate.
A waste gas released during the breakdown of pyruvate.
An energy-carrying molecule that holds high-energy electrons.
A key molecule formed from pyruvate that enters the next stage of cellular respiration.
A helper molecule that attaches to an acetyl group to carry it to the next pathway.

diagram_alt_text: Diagram (Figure 7.10) illustrating the three-step breakdown of pyruvate. Pyruvate enters from the cytosol across the outer and inner membranes into the mitochondrial matrix via a pyruvate carrier protein. Step 1 shows CO2 being released. Step 2 shows NAD+ picking up electrons to form NADH and H+. Step 3 shows Coenzyme A attaching to form Acetyl CoA.
